# Column Value Validations {#sec-column-validations}

```{python}
#| include: false
import pointblank as pb
pb.config(report_incl_header=False, report_incl_footer=False)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Compact validation reports
This chapter shows a validation report for almost every example, because seeing the result is the
point. To keep those reports compact we hide the header and footer with
`pb.config(report_incl_header=False, report_incl_footer=False)`, which leaves just the step rows. In
your own work you will usually want the header and footer visible for the context they add.
:::

Most data quality problems show up in column values. You might find a negative number in a revenue
column, for example, or an empty cell in a field that is supposed to be required. Column value
validations catch problems like these by stating what you expect in a column and checking every row
against it.

This chapter covers Pointblank's column value methods in detail. It is the longest chapter in the
book because these are the methods you will use most. For each family we look at more than one
example, cover the edge cases that tend to trip people up, and talk about when to pick one method
over another. Toward the end we look at column selectors, which let one step cover many columns,
and the `dimension=` argument, which ties a check to the quality scoring of @sec-quality-scoring.

Two built-in datasets carry us through. The `game_revenue` table has a realistic mix of numeric,
categorical, and identifier columns across 2,000 rows. The smaller `small_table` is useful when we
want a result short enough to count by hand. A few tiny hand-built frames also appear, for cases
where it is easier to construct an edge case than to go looking for one in real data.

```{python}
game_revenue = pb.load_dataset(dataset="game_revenue", tbl_type="polars")
small_table = pb.load_dataset(dataset="small_table", tbl_type="polars")

pb.preview(game_revenue)
```

The columns we will come back to most are the numeric `session_duration` and `item_revenue`, the
categorical `item_type` and `acquisition`, and the identifiers `player_id` and `session_id`. Let's
start checking them.

## Comparison validations

The most basic column checks compare each value against a fixed value or against another column.
There are six of them, one for each of the usual comparison operators, and they all take the same
arguments: `columns=` for what to check, `value=` for what to compare against, and `na_pass=` for
how to treat nulls.

### Greater than and less than

The `col_vals_gt()` method checks that values are greater than a given value. A good first use is
asserting something you believe is always true, such as every session having a positive duration.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=game_revenue)
    .col_vals_gt(columns="session_duration", value=0)
    .interrogate()
)
```

All 2,000 test units pass (the shortest session in the table is 3.2). A check that passes may not
seem to tell you much, but it will fail on the day an upstream change lets a zero or negative
duration through. Often, though, you choose a comparison value to pick out a
particular set of rows rather than to confirm something universal. Here we raise the bar to a
revenue greater than 1.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=game_revenue)
    .col_vals_gt(columns="item_revenue", value=1)
    .interrogate()
)
```

Now 604 rows pass and 1,396 fail. That is not a sign of bad data. Most rows in this table are ad
impressions, which typically earn a small fraction of a unit, while in-app purchases usually earn
more. The split is not perfectly clean, though: 172 ad rows earn more than 1, and 15 in-app
purchases earn 1 or less. The counterpart, `col_vals_lt()`, checks an upper bound in the same way.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=game_revenue)
    .col_vals_lt(columns="session_duration", value=40)
    .interrogate()
)
```

Here 74 of the 2,000 sessions have a duration of 40 or more and fail. Note that `col_vals_gt()` and
`col_vals_lt()` are strict, so a value exactly equal to the comparison value fails. A session with
a duration of exactly 40 would fail `col_vals_lt(value=40)`, because 40 is not less than 40. When
the boundary value should count as acceptable, you need the inclusive versions, which are covered
next.

### Inclusive versus strict bounds

The `col_vals_ge()` and `col_vals_le()` methods are the inclusive versions, meaning the boundary
value passes. You only see a difference when a value sits exactly on the boundary, so let's make a
tiny frame that contains a zero.

```{python}
import polars as pl

boundary = pl.DataFrame({"x": [0, 1, 2]})

(
    pb.Validate(data=boundary)
    .col_vals_gt(columns="x", value=0)
    .interrogate()
)
```

The strict `col_vals_gt(value=0)` fails the row with `0` and passes the rows with `1` and `2`. Now
the inclusive version:

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=boundary)
    .col_vals_ge(columns="x", value=0)
    .interrogate()
)
```

All three rows pass, because `col_vals_ge()` accepts `0` as meeting the bound. To choose between
the two forms, ask whether the boundary value itself is valid. A stock count of zero for a sold-out
product is a perfectly valid value, for instance, and the strict form would wrongly flag it. Revenue
works the same way, so a non-negativity check on revenue should be inclusive.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=game_revenue)
    .col_vals_ge(columns="item_revenue", value=0)
    .interrogate()
)
```

Every row passes. As it happens, `game_revenue` has no zero-revenue rows (the smallest value is
0.004), so the strict and inclusive forms would give the same answer on this data. Using
`col_vals_ge()` is still the right call, since it states the actual rule and will not fail if a
free item shows up later.

### Equality and inequality

The `col_vals_eq()` and `col_vals_ne()` methods check that values are equal, or not equal, to a
given value. The `item_type` column holds only `"ad"` and `"iap"`, so checking that every row equals
`"iap"` splits the table in two.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=game_revenue)
    .col_vals_eq(columns="item_type", value="iap")
    .interrogate()
)
```

There are 447 passing rows and 1,553 failing ones, the failures being the ad rows. In practice,
equality is most useful when a column should hold a single constant, like a currency code that
should always be `"USD"` in a domestic feed. The `col_vals_ne()` method forbids one specific value.
Because `item_type` has only two values, checking that it is never `"ad"` gives exactly the same
result as the check above: 447 passing and 1,553 failing.

Be careful using `col_vals_eq()` with floating-point numbers. The comparison is exact, and a value
computed with arithmetic often does not exactly equal the number you would write for it.

```{python}
computed = pl.DataFrame({"x": [0.1 + 0.2]})

(
    pb.Validate(data=computed)
    .col_vals_eq(columns="x", value=0.3)
    .interrogate()
)
```

The single row fails, because `0.1 + 0.2` comes out very slightly different from `0.3`. This is not
something Pointblank is doing. It is how floating-point arithmetic works, and it means
`col_vals_eq()` is the wrong tool for computed decimals. To confirm that a computed value matches an
expected one, allow a small tolerance, either by checking that the value falls within a narrow range
or by writing an expression that compares with a tolerance (an approach covered in
@sec-advanced-validation). Keep `col_vals_eq()` for exact values like integers, strings, and
category codes.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why `0.1 + 0.2` is not `0.3`

Computers store most decimals in binary floating point. Just as one third has no exact finite
decimal form, numbers like 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary form, so each is stored as the nearest
value the format can represent. Those tiny rounding errors carry through arithmetic, and `0.1 + 0.2`
ends up slightly away from the stored value of `0.3`. Nearly every programming language uses this
format for decimals, so comparing computed decimals for exact equality is a mistake everywhere, not
just in Python or Pointblank.
:::

### Comparing against another column

The comparison value does not have to be a constant. If you wrap a column name in `pb.col()`, each
row is compared against the value in that other column. This is how you check relationships between
columns, such as a sale price being higher than its cost or an end date coming after a start date.
Using `small_table`, we can check whether each value in column `a` is less than the value in column
`c`.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=small_table)
    .col_vals_lt(columns="a", value=pb.col("c"), na_pass=True)
    .interrogate()
)
```

Eight of the 13 rows pass and five fail, those being the rows where `a` is not less than `c`. Every
comparison method accepts `pb.col()` in place of a literal value, so "the sale price is greater than
the cost" becomes `col_vals_gt(columns="sale_price", value=pb.col("cost"))` and "the ship date is on
or after the order date" becomes `col_vals_ge(columns="ship_date", value=pb.col("order_date"))`. We
set `na_pass=True` here because column `c` has two nulls. Without it, those two rows would also
fail and the result would be 6 passing and 7 failing. How nulls are treated in comparisons is the
topic of the next section.

### Handling nulls in comparisons

Every comparison method has an `na_pass=` argument that decides what happens when a value is null.
The default is `False`, which means a null counts as a failure: a missing value cannot be shown to
meet the condition. Column `c` of `small_table` has two nulls, so we can see this with a check that
values are at most 10.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=small_table)
    .col_vals_le(columns="c", value=10)
    .interrogate()
)
```

Eleven rows pass and two fail. The two failures are not values above 10. They are the two nulls. If
we set `na_pass=True`, nulls count as passing instead.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=small_table)
    .col_vals_le(columns="c", value=10, na_pass=True)
    .interrogate()
)
```

Now all 13 rows pass, since the 11 non-null values are all at most 10 and the two nulls are let
through. Which setting is right depends on what a null means in your data. If a null means "not
applicable", such as a sale price that is null because the item is not on sale, then
`na_pass=True` is correct because the check does not apply to that row. If a null means a value
that should be there but is missing, keep the default, because then one step catches both
out-of-range values and unexpected gaps. If missingness is the thing you want
to measure, the methods in @sec-missing-data are a better fit than toggling `na_pass=`.

## Range validations

You could keep values within a range using two comparisons, one for the lower bound and one for the
upper bound. A range validation does the same job in one step, and its report is easier to read
because both bounds appear together instead of being spread across two steps.

### Between

The `col_vals_between()` method checks that values fall within a range, and both ends are inclusive
by default. Column `a` in `small_table` runs from 1 to 8, so a check with those bounds passes.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=small_table)
    .col_vals_between(columns="a", left=1, right=8)
    .interrogate()
)
```

All 13 rows pass. Because both ends are inclusive, the rows with exactly 1 and exactly 8 are
accepted, which is usually what a rule like "ages between 18 and 65" means. The `inclusive=`
argument controls this with a pair of booleans for the left and right ends. Setting both to `False`
excludes the endpoints.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=small_table)
    .col_vals_between(columns="a", left=1, right=8, inclusive=(False, False))
    .interrogate()
)
```

Now 11 rows pass and two fail. The failures are the row where `a` is 1 and the row where it is 8,
since the endpoints are no longer part of the range. The two ends are set independently, so
`inclusive=(True, False)` accepts the lower bound but not the upper, which suits a rule like "at
least 0 and less than 100 percent". As with the comparison methods, either bound can be a
`pb.col()` reference, so you can check that a value sits between a per-row minimum and maximum. On
`game_revenue`, a plausibility range for session duration gives a more typical mixed result.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=game_revenue)
    .col_vals_between(columns="session_duration", left=5, right=40)
    .interrogate()
)
```

Here 1,915 rows fall between 5 and 40 and 85 fall outside. Of those 85, 14 are sessions shorter
than 5 and 71 are longer than 40. Compare that with the 74 failures from `col_vals_lt(value=40)`
earlier: three sessions last exactly 40, which the inclusive range accepts but the strict
comparison rejected. These very short and very long sessions are the ones worth a closer look.

### Outside

The `col_vals_outside()` method is the reverse. It passes values outside a range and fails values
inside it. Let's check that column `a` lies outside the range 3 to 6.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=small_table)
    .col_vals_outside(columns="a", left=3, right=6)
    .interrogate()
)
```

Six rows pass because their values are below 3 or above 6, and seven fail because they fall between
3 and 6. Checking that values lie outside a range can seem backward, but it is a natural way to flag
anomalies. If a range of numeric codes is reserved for errors, for example, any value inside that
range deserves attention. Like `col_vals_between()`, this method takes an `inclusive=` pair that
controls whether the endpoints count as inside the range.

## Set membership validations

Ranges suit numeric data, but categorical columns need a different kind of check. When a column's
values come from a fixed list, such as a set of status codes, the right question is whether each
value is on that list.

### In set

The `col_vals_in_set()` method checks that each value belongs to a set of allowed values. The
`item_type` column should only ever contain `"iap"` or `"ad"`.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=game_revenue)
    .col_vals_in_set(columns="item_type", set=["iap", "ad"])
    .interrogate()
)
```

Every row passes, so there are no unexpected values in the column. Keep in mind that the matching
is exact, so a value like `"IAP"` or `"iap "` (with a trailing space) would fail. The
`acquisition` column has six channels, and if we list only three of them we can see failures.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=game_revenue)
    .col_vals_in_set(columns="acquisition", set=["organic", "facebook", "google"])
    .interrogate()
)
```

There are 1,594 passing rows and 406 failing ones, the failures being rows from the three channels
we left out (`other_campaign`, `crosspromo`, and `apple`). It is worth knowing how this check treats
a null, since a null is not one of the listed values. A small frame shows what happens.

```{python}
with_null = pl.DataFrame({"s": ["a", "b", None]})

(
    pb.Validate(data=with_null)
    .col_vals_in_set(columns="s", set=["a", "b"])
    .interrogate()
)
```

Two rows pass and the null row fails, because the null is not in the set. If nulls are acceptable in
the column, add `None` to the set itself (`set=["a", "b", None]` passes all three rows here). You can also
pass a Python `Enum` as the `set=`, which lets you keep the list of allowed values in one place in
your code.

### Not in set

The `col_vals_not_in_set()` method works the other way, failing any value that appears in a
forbidden set. This is useful when the list of valid values is too long or open-ended to write out,
but you know a few specific values that indicate a problem, such as codes for discontinued products.
Let's forbid the value `other_campaign` in the `acquisition` column.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=game_revenue)
    .col_vals_not_in_set(columns="acquisition", set=["other_campaign"])
    .interrogate()
)
```

There are 1,733 passing rows and 267 failing ones, which is every row tagged with `other_campaign`.

## Null validations

Missing values are one of the most common data quality problems, and whether a null is acceptable
depends on the column. Pointblank has a method for each case: one that requires values to be
present and one that requires them to be absent.

### Requiring values to be present

The `col_vals_not_null()` method checks that a required column has a value in every row. Both
identifier columns in `game_revenue` should always be filled in.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=game_revenue)
    .col_vals_not_null(columns="player_id")
    .col_vals_not_null(columns="session_id")
    .interrogate()
)
```

Both steps pass for all 2,000 rows, so no identifiers are missing. Running the same check on column
`c` of `small_table` finds its two nulls.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=small_table)
    .col_vals_not_null(columns="c")
    .interrogate()
)
```

Eleven rows pass and two fail. This is probably the most common validation of all, since a missing
value in a required column tends to cause trouble in everything downstream of it.

### Requiring values to be absent

The `col_vals_null()` method checks the opposite, that a column is empty. You will need this less
often, but it is useful when null is the correct value, such as an activation date that should stay
unset for archived records, or a derived field that should not be filled in yet at a certain stage
of a pipeline. Here is a small table where the column is all nulls.

```{python}
archived = pl.DataFrame({"active_date": [None, None, None]}, schema={"active_date": pl.Datetime})

(
    pb.Validate(data=archived)
    .col_vals_null(columns="active_date")
    .interrogate()
)
```

All three rows pass because every value is null, as expected. The two null methods are exact
opposites. A column that is partly filled in and partly empty fails both of them:
`col_vals_not_null()` fails on the empty rows and `col_vals_null()` fails on the filled ones.

## Pattern matching

Numeric bounds and set membership do not help much with structured text. Many text columns, like
product codes, follow a fixed format, and the usual way to check a format is with a regular
expression.

### Regular expressions

The `col_vals_regex()` method checks that text values match a regular expression, written in
standard Python syntax. Column `b` in `small_table` holds values like `"1-bcd-345"`: a digit, three
lowercase letters, and three digits, separated by hyphens. We can require exactly that format.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=small_table)
    .col_vals_regex(columns="b", pattern=r"^\d-[a-z]{3}-\d{3}$")
    .interrogate()
)
```

All 13 rows pass, so the column is consistently formatted. In the pattern, `^` marks the start of
the string, `\d` is a single digit, `[a-z]{3}` is three lowercase letters, `\d{3}` is three digits,
and `$` marks the end, so any value that strays from this format fails. The method also has an `inverse=` argument that flips the check so that rows
matching the pattern fail. That turns a pattern into a blocklist. Here we reject the value `"high"`
in column `f`.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=small_table)
    .col_vals_regex(columns="f", pattern="high", inverse=True)
    .interrogate()
)
```

Seven rows pass and six fail, and the six failures are exactly the rows where `f` is `"high"`. Like
the comparison methods, `col_vals_regex()` accepts `na_pass=` to control how nulls are handled.
Regular expressions are powerful but can be hard to read, and for common formats there is an easier
option, which the next section covers.

## Validating against known formats

Some common formats are awkward to express as a regular expression, especially ones that include a
checksum or vary by country. The `col_vals_within_spec()` method checks a column against a named
specification and handles those details for you. Here is a short list of email addresses, some
valid and some not.

```{python}
contacts = pl.DataFrame({
    "email": [
        "grace@example.org",
        "silly-sarah@example.com",
        "not-an-email",
        "bob@bad",
        "carol@example.io",
    ]
})

(
    pb.Validate(data=contacts)
    .col_vals_within_spec(columns="email", spec="email")
    .interrogate()
)
```

Three of the five rows pass. The two failures are `"not-an-email"`, which has no `@` or domain at
all, and `"bob@bad"`, which has no top-level domain. The real advantage of a specification is that
it can check things a pattern cannot. The credit card specification, for example, applies the Luhn
checksum, so it can tell a number that only has the right number of digits from one whose digits
actually check out.

```{python}
cards = pl.DataFrame({"card": ["4111111111111111", "5500005555555559", "4111111111111112"]})

(
    pb.Validate(data=cards)
    .col_vals_within_spec(columns="card", spec="credit_card")
    .interrogate()
)
```

Two rows pass and the third fails. It has 16 digits like the others, but its Luhn checksum is wrong,
which no digit-count pattern could detect. Some specifications depend on the country, and postal
codes are one of them, so you include the country in the spec name.

```{python}
zips = pl.DataFrame({"zip": ["90210", "12345", "9021", "ABCDE"]})

(
    pb.Validate(data=zips)
    .col_vals_within_spec(columns="zip", spec="postal_code[USA]")
    .interrogate()
)
```
